chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Jamhur from Ahmad ibn al-Husayn from his father from Ismail ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Sinan who said:

I was in the presence of al-Rida (peace be upon him), so he said to me: 'O Muhammad! Indeed, in the time of the Children of Israel, there were four believers. One of them came to the other three, who were gathered in the house of one of them, engaged in a discussion among themselves. He knocked on the door, and the slave came out to him. He said, 'Where is your master?' He said, 'He is not in the house.'

The man returned, and the slave went to his master. He said to him, 'Who was the one who knocked on the door?' He said, 'So-and-so.' I told him, 'You are not in the house.' So he remained silent and did not care, and he did not blame his slave, nor was any of them saddened by his return from the door, and they continued in their conversation.

When it was the next day, the man came early to them and found them, and they had gone out intending a property of one of them. He greeted them and said, 'I am with you.' They said to him, 'Yes,' and they did not apologize to him. The man was needy and of weak financial state. When they were on part of the way, a cloud shaded them, and they thought it was rain, so they hastened.

When the cloud settled directly over their heads, a caller called out from within the cloud: 'O Fire! Seize them, and I am Jibra'il, the Messenger of Allah!' So a fire from within the cloud snatched the three men, and the man remained terrified, amazed at what had befallen the people, and he did not know the reason.

So he returned to the city and met Yusha' ibn Nun (peace be upon him) and informed him of the news and what he had seen and heard. Yusha' ibn Nun (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you not know that Allah was pleased with them, but then became angry with them, and that was due to their deed with you?' He said, 'And what was their deed with me?' So Yusha' narrated it to him. The man said, 'So I hereby make them free and excuse them.' He said: 'Had this been before, it would have benefited them, but as for now, no. And perhaps it might benefit them afterwards.'
ai.seo_question: What is the consequence of excluding a believer from a gathering without apology?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) uses this narrative to illustrate the specific sin of *al-istidraj* or divine displeasure resulting from excluding a needy brother without justification, a key concept in Shia ethics regarding social solidarity. The story highlights that while the three believers were punished for their arrogance and neglect, the fourth’s subsequent offer of pardon (*al-'afw*) was accepted as a potential intercession, demonstrating the enduring power of forgiveness even after judgment has commenced.
